posts.title: New Jersey Real Estate Market 2026: What Buyers, Sellers & Renters Need to Know
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: A clear breakdown of New Jersey's 2026 real estate trends — housing, rentals, and commercial — and what they mean depending on where you sit in the market.
posts.content:
New Jersey Real Estate in 2026: What Buyers, Sellers, and Renters Need to Know

Whether you're house-hunting, thinking about selling, or just trying to understand why your rent went up again, New Jersey's 2026 real estate market has a clearer story than the headlines suggest. Here's what's actually happening, sector by sector.

The overall mood: cautious confidence. After a volatile but ultimately active 2025, industry forecasters (Real Estate NJ's 2026 outlook among them) describe this year as one of "conviction in fundamentals" — meaning buyers and sellers are operating with more realistic expectations, and deals are getting done rather than stalling out over pricing standoffs.

For buyers: Multifamily and residential transaction volume in North Jersey is expected to surpass 2025, marking the most active stretch since 2022. That means more competition in some segments, but also more realistic pricing from sellers who understand the market has shifted. Rent growth has moderated, which is a meaningful signal if you've been priced out of buying and are watching the rental market instead.

For sellers: Demand remains real, particularly for properties near transit and employment centers — a pattern that's held steady in New Jersey for years and shows no sign of reversing. If your property fits that profile, 2026 forecasts suggest a genuinely active pool of buyers.

For renters: Moderating rent growth is good news, but supply constraints haven't disappeared. New Jersey's affordable housing legislation (commonly referenced as "A4") is creating rezoning requirements that could add thousands of new units over time — a longer-term factor worth watching rather than something that changes your search this year.

What about commercial and industrial? Industrial real estate posted positive net absorption for the first time in over a year, with limited new supply supporting healthy fundamentals — good news if you're a small business owner considering warehouse or light-industrial space. Retail has proven more resilient than expected, especially neighborhood centers anchored by food and service businesses. Office space remains the most uncertain category, though Class A, transit-oriented properties with strong amenities continue to perform.

"New Jersey's 2026 market isn't a boom or a correction — it's a return to buyers and sellers actually agreeing on reality." — WAJ Editorial Team

The bottom line: 2026 looks like a more balanced New Jersey market than the last few years — real opportunity for buyers and sellers who come in with realistic expectations, and a rental market where growth is finally slowing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is 2026 a good year to buy a house in New Jersey? Market forecasters point to increased transaction volume and more realistic pricing, but individual decisions depend on your local market, budget, and timeline — talk to a licensed NJ real estate professional about your specific situation.

Are NJ rents going down in 2026? Rent growth has moderated according to industry forecasts, but that's not the same as rents falling — supply constraints remain a factor in many areas.

What is New Jersey's affordable housing legislation (A4)? It's state legislation creating rezoning requirements aimed at increasing housing supply; consult official state and municipal sources for how it applies to a specific town.

posts.title: Jersey Club 101: The History and Sound of Newark's Signature Genre
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Where Jersey Club came from, what makes the sound distinct, and why it's having another viral moment — a beginner's guide to New Jersey's biggest musical export.
posts.content:
Jersey Club 101: The Sound That Started in Newark and Took Over the World

If you've heard a song with a rapid, bouncing kick pattern and a chopped-up vocal sample that makes you want to move — and it felt distinctly different from the club music coming out of any other city — there's a good chance it was Jersey Club. It's one of New Jersey's most influential cultural exports, and it started right in Newark.

Where it came from. Jersey Club grew out of Newark's club and DJ scene in the late 1990s and early 2000s, evolving out of Baltimore club music but developing its own signature tempo, triplet-heavy kick patterns, and vocal-chop style. DJs and producers based in and around Newark — widely credited pioneers include DJ Tameil, one of the genre's founding figures, alongside the broader Brick City DJ community — built the sound in local clubs and mixtapes long before streaming platforms existed.

What makes it distinct. Jersey Club typically sits around 130-140 BPM, built on a signature "bed squeak" and triplet kick pattern, chopped vocal samples (often pulled from pop, R&B, or hip-hop hits), and a stripped-down, dance-floor-first production style. It's music built for movement first — the genre grew alongside a distinct style of dance that spread through New Jersey and mid-Atlantic clubs and school gyms.

Why it's having a moment again. Music press covering electronic and club genres (Bandcamp Daily, Future Audio Workshop, and others) has documented a renewed wave of attention on Jersey Club in recent years, as producers reinterpret pop and hip-hop tracks in the Jersey Club style and the genre finds new audiences on streaming and short-form video. ⚠️ Because the artist landscape shifts quickly and WAJ has not independently confirmed current lineups, tour dates, or new releases beyond what's cited here, treat any specific current-artist claims as needing verification before publishing a follow-up piece.

Where to actually hear it in New Jersey. Jersey Club lives in local club nights, DJ sets, and community events across Essex County and beyond — WAJ recommends checking with Newark-area venues and event promoters directly for current listings rather than relying on outdated event calendars.

"Jersey Club isn't a trend that visited New Jersey — it's a sound that was born here and never left." — WAJ Editorial Team

The bottom line: Jersey Club is a homegrown New Jersey genre with real staying power and global reach. Understanding its Newark roots is the starting point for appreciating why it keeps resurfacing in mainstream music.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Jersey Club the same as Baltimore Club? No — Jersey Club evolved from Baltimore Club music but developed its own distinct tempo, kick pattern, and production style specific to Newark and the surrounding area.

Who are the pioneers of Jersey Club? DJ Tameil is widely credited as a founding figure, developing the sound within Newark's DJ community; the genre grew through a broader collective of Brick City-based producers and DJs.

Where can I hear Jersey Club live in New Jersey today? Check directly with Newark-area club nights, DJ collectives, and event promoters for current listings, since specific venues and dates change frequently.

posts.title: How to Start a Small Business in New Jersey (2026 Guide)
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: A step-by-step guide to starting a small business in New Jersey in 2026 — registration, funding, grants, and free state resources, explained clearly.
posts.content:
How to Start a Small Business in New Jersey: A Complete 2026 Guide

New Jersey's entrepreneurs are building everything from Jersey Shore food trucks to Newark tech startups, and the state has put real infrastructure behind that momentum. If you're ready to turn an idea into a registered business, here's what the process actually looks like in 2026 — and where to find help along the way.

Start with the state's free planning tools. Business.NJ.gov, New Jersey's official small-business portal, offers a "Navigator" tool that builds a personalized starter kit based on your business type, walking you through registration requirements, tax obligations, and funding options in one place. The site also publishes a Small Business Manual (available in print and digital form) and offers live chat support with actual state representatives — a genuinely useful first stop before you spend money on a consultant.

Choose and register your business structure. Most new NJ businesses register as an LLC, S-corp, or sole proprietorship through the state's Division of Revenue and Enterprise Services. Your structure affects your taxes, liability, and how you'll eventually raise money, so this is worth ten minutes of real research (or a call to a free SCORE mentor) rather than a guess.

Look into funding before you assume you need a bank loan. New Jersey has multiple small-business grant and loan programs run through the NJEDA and other state partners, and eligibility changes year to year. ⚠️ Because specific grant names, amounts, and deadlines shift frequently, confirm current programs directly at business.nj.gov before including specifics in outreach to readers — this article intentionally points to the live resource rather than listing amounts that could be outdated by the time you read this.

Get local before you get big. New Jersey's chambers of commerce, county economic development offices, and business improvement districts often have more responsive, hyper-local support than state-level programs — and they're a natural source of your first customers. If you're a WAJ reader building a business anywhere from Bergen to Cape May counties, consider this your reminder to introduce yourself to your local chamber early.

Build your online presence with intention. A Google Business Profile, a simple website, and a consistent handle across Instagram and TikTok matter more for discoverability than most new founders expect — and they're free or low-cost to set up correctly from day one.

"The businesses that last in New Jersey aren't the ones with the biggest launch — they're the ones that show up for their community, week after week." — WAJ Editorial Team

The bottom line: New Jersey gives founders real, free tools to start smart. Use Business.NJ.gov as your foundation, register correctly the first time, and lean on local networks before you scale.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need an LLC to start a small business in New Jersey? Not necessarily — sole proprietorships are simpler to start, but an LLC offers liability protection many founders want once they're taking on customers or employees. Consult a business attorney or accountant for your specific situation.

How much does it cost to register a business in New Jersey? Costs vary by structure and are set by the state; confirm current filing fees directly at business.nj.gov before budgeting, since fee schedules can change.

Where can I find New Jersey small business grants? Business.NJ.gov's funding library and the NJEDA are the most reliable, current starting points — verify eligibility and deadlines directly on those sites rather than through secondhand roundups.

posts.title: U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester, Mayor John Carney, New Castle County Executive Marcus Henry to Open the YDC
posts.author: Desiree P. Bell
posts.summary: Federal, State, Local and Community Leaders Unite to Celebrate Grand Opening of Community Education Building’s Youth Development Center at YDC Fest. U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester, Mayor John Carney, New Castle County Executive Marcus Henry and other leaders will join families and community partners to mark the opening of a transformative new hub for Wilmington’s youth.
posts.content:
WHAT
Free, family-centered celebration will showcase a new home for education, wellness, arts, athletics and family resources — supporting young people from cradle to career

The Community Education Building (CEB) will officially celebrate the grand opening of its new Youth Development Center (YDC) with YDC Fest, a free, family-centered community celebration on Friday, August 21.
More than a festival, YDC Fest marks the opening of a transformative new community asset designed to bring education, wellness, arts, athletics and family resources together under one roof — creating opportunities for Wilmington’s young people and families from cradle to career.

The celebration will feature live music and performing arts, sports demonstrations, back-to-school giveaways, family resources, interactive activities, free food, raffles and experiences led by more than a dozen community organizations.

The festivities will start with a community procession, that ends at the new Youth Development Center. Please see map HERE
A formal grand opening program will begin at 2:00 p.m. and bring together federal, state and local elected officials, community leaders, partners and youth voices to celebrate this significant investment in Wilmington’s young people and families.

MEDIA RSVP
Media are asked to RSVP by Thursday, August 20 at 10:00 a.m. ET.  to dpbell@desirepeterkinbell.com
 

WHO
Mistress of Ceremonies:
Ihsan Muhammad, Chief Strategy Officer, Community Education Building
Scheduled Speakers and Participants:

    Linda Jennings, CEO, Community Education Building
    Mayor John Carney, City of Wilmington
    U.S. Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester
    New Castle County Executive Marcus Henry
    State Senator S. Elizabeth “Tizzy” Lockman
    State Representative Stephanie T. Bolden
    Zanthia Oliver, Wilmington City Council Member, 3rd District
    Luke Kenenske, GGA Construction
    Ben Garvin, Fearn Clendaniel Architects
    Amali Holloway, Student

Representatives from YDC resident and community partners, sponsors, families, students and members of the greater Wilmington community will also participate.


WHEN
Friday, August 21, 2026
YDC Fest: 1:00–6:00 p.m.
Procession: 1pm.
Formal Grand Opening Program: 2:00 p.m.

WHERE
Youth Development Center
315 East 12th Street
Wilmington, DE

VISUALS / MEDIA OPPORTUNITIES
Media will have opportunities to capture:

    Federal, state and local elected officials alongside community leaders and youth
    Grand opening remarks and celebration
    Families and young people experiencing the Youth Development Center
    Live music and performing arts
    Sports demonstrations and youth activities
    Back-to-school giveaways
    Community organizations providing resources and interactive experiences
    The new 42,000-square-foot facility, including its gymnasium, smart classrooms, black box theater and performing arts space, fitness room, youth lounge and flexible programming spaces

MEDIA RSVP
Media are asked to RSVP by Thursday, August 20 at 10:00 a.m. ET.  to dpbell@desirepeterkinbell.com
 
ABOUT CEB
The Community Education Building (CEB) is a Wilmington, Delaware-based nonprofit advancing education equity through an innovative cradle-to-career ecosystem that connects education, youth development, wellness, and family support. Through its collaborative co-location model, CEB brings schools, nonprofit organizations, families, and community partners together to remove barriers, expand opportunity, and create pathways to long-term success.

At the heart of this ecosystem is the 42,000-square-foot Youth Development Center (YDC), a dynamic hub featuring smart classrooms, a black box theater and performing arts space, full gymnasium, fitness room, youth lounge, and flexible spaces for learning and community programming. The YDC expands CEB’s network of trusted partners to support Wilmington’s young people from their earliest years through adulthood.

As the YDC’s anchor resident partner, the YMCA of Delaware operates its Early Learning Academy, providing high-quality early childhood education for up to 100 children from infancy through pre-K. Together, CEB, the YDC, and their partners are building a connected pathway from strong beginnings to limitless potential for Wilmington’s children, families, and community.

posts.author: Desiree P. Bell
posts.summary:
Community Education Building to Celebrate Grand Opening of the Youth Development Center with YDC Fest on August 21.
Free, family-centered festival will welcome Wilmington to a new home for education, wellness, arts, athletics, and family resources — supporting young people from cradle to career
posts.content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
 
Community Education Building to Celebrate Grand Opening of the Youth Development Center with YDC Fest on August 21
 
Free, family-centered festival will welcome Wilmington to a new home for education, wellness, arts, athletics, and family resources — supporting young people from cradle to career
 

WILMINGTON, DE — The Community Education Building (CEB) today announced YDC Fest, a community celebration and grand opening of the Youth Development Center, taking place Friday, August 21, from 1–6 PM. The free, family-friendly event marks the first time the greater Wilmington community will be welcomed onto the new campus. A short formal program will take place at 2pm with elected and community leaders.
 
More than a festival, YDC Fest celebrates the opening of a new community asset — one designed to bring education, wellness, arts, athletics, and family resources together under one roof to support Wilmington's young people at every stage, from cradle to career.
 
"This is more than a building opening — it's the opening of new possibilities for our children and families," said Linda Jennings, CEO of the Community Education Building. "The Youth Development Center represents what's possible when a community comes together around a shared belief: that every young person deserves the resources, support, and opportunity to thrive. We can't wait to welcome Wilmington home on August 21."
 
A Day for the Whole Family
 
Attendees can look forward to a full day of activities, including:
 

    Back-to-school giveaways
    Live music and performing arts
    Sports demonstrations
    Family resources and interactive activities
    Free food and raffles
    Experiences led by more than a dozen community organizations

 
The event will feature activations from resident and community partners, including YMCA of Delaware, Kuumba Academy Charter School, Christina Cultural Arts Center, Delaware Sensory Museum, Delaware Health Empowerment Coalition, Network Connect, Great Oaks Charter School, CSC Global, Delaware Youth Sports Coalition, and many more — bringing to life the collaborative model that makes the Youth Development Center unlike anything else in Wilmington.
 
 
 
Made Possible by Community Investment
 
YDC Fest is made possible by a coalition of organizations investing in Wilmington's future:
 

    Founding Sponsor: GGA Construction
    Gold Sponsors: Nemours Children's Health; Anthony & Catherine Fusco Foundation, Grow America
    Silver Sponsor: Barclays US Consumer Bank
    Bronze Sponsor: REACH Riverside, Bank of America, Saul Ewing
    Community Sponsors: Fearn Clendaniel Architects, Delaware Elevator, New Castle Insurance, Wawa, WSFS

 
Together, these partners are helping ensure YDC Fest remains a free, family-centered celebration that welcomes the greater Wilmington community into the Youth Development Center for the very first time.
 
Get Involved
 
Families are encouraged to pre-register by scanning the QR code on the event flyer or using this link. Youth under the age of 17 must be supervised by an adult. Community members can help spread the word by sharing the event with their networks in the lead-up to August 21.
 
"Together, we're opening more than a building — we're opening new opportunities for Wilmington's youth and families," Jennings added.
 
Event Details
What: YDC Fest — Youth Development Center Grand Opening Celebration
When: Friday, August 21, 1–6 PM
Where: 315 East 12th street Youth Development Center, Wilmington, DE
Cost: Free and open to the public; pre-registration encouraged

The Community Education Building (CEB) is a Wilmington, Delaware-based nonprofit advancing education equity through an innovative cradle-to-career ecosystem that connects education, youth development, wellness, and family support. Through its collaborative co-location model, CEB brings schools, nonprofit organizations, families, and community partners together to remove barriers, expand opportunity, and create pathways to long-term success.
 
At the heart of this ecosystem is the 42,000-square-foot Youth Development Center (YDC), a dynamic hub featuring smart classrooms, a black box theater and performing arts space, full gymnasium, fitness room, youth lounge, and flexible spaces for learning and community programming. The YDC expands CEB’s network of trusted partners to support Wilmington’s young people from their earliest years through adulthood.  As the YDC’s anchor resident partner, the YMCA of Delaware operates its Early Learning Academy, providing high-quality early childhood education for up to 100 children from infancy through pre-K. Together, CEB, the YDC, and their partners are building a connected pathway from strong beginnings to limitless potential for Wilmington’s children, families, and community.

posts.title: Middlesex County Presents the 2026 Gospel Music Festival with Grammy-Winning Superstars Erica Campbell and Jonathan McReynolds
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: MIDDLESEX COUNTY, NJ – Middlesex County, as part of its FolkLIVE free community event series, will present its third annual Gospel Music Festival in New Brunswi…
posts.content:
MIDDLESEX COUNTY, NJ – Middlesex County, as part of its FolkLIVE free community event series, will present its third annual Gospel Music Festival in New Brunswick, NJ (2 Livingston Ave.) on Saturday, July 25, 2026, from 3:30 pm to 7:30 pm. This year’s star-studded lineup features Grammy Award-winning performers Erica Campbell and Jonathan McReynolds as headliners, joined by Billboard chart-topping gospel group The Group Fire from Newark. The lineup also includes talented local artists Tangie Cobb, Valarie Adams, Bishop George C. Searight & Royal Priesthood, Myles Cherrette, and DJ RunTheFade. This free, outdoor concert celebrates African American cultural heritage through an afternoon of gospel music and will be emceed by Toya Beasley, host of 94.7 The Block, and nationally recognized arts administrator Deonté Griffin-Quick.

New exciting updates to amenities for attendees:

    The New Brunswick Performing Arts Center (NBPAC), adjacent to the festival, will serve as a cooling center and provide a live streaming option of the event.
    The Heldrich Hotel and Conference Center is offering a promotional rate of $119/per night for concertgoers to make the most of the event with group code: 665687 (valid until 7/3/2026).
    Food and beverage vendors will be on-site, including Delta’s Patty Wagon, McGriff’s Fish and Chips, Just Pies by Lisa, Devvon’s Lemonade, and Jamaica Taste.
    Free and paid parking facilities will be available, and Middlesex County RIDE shuttles will transport guests from parking areas to the event location.
    The event is also accessible via mass transit on the NJ TRANSIT Northeast Corridor Line and Amtrak, exit at New Brunswick station.
    The County encourages the attendees to bring their own lawn chairs, sun protection, and cooling accessories. For full details, visit the MiddlesexCountyCulture.com event listing, click here.

“In Middlesex County, we know that access to free and affordable arts and culture can transform a community,” said Middlesex County Commissioner Director Ronald G. Rios. “Events like the annual Gospel Music Festival transcend race and religion; it’s a cultural event that unites and inspires people from all backgrounds with a common passion to learn, celebrate, and immerse in live music.”

“FolkLIVE Gospel Music Festival is an event dear to my heart and is a beautiful expression of what is possible when we open our minds to the rich diversity of our County,” said Middlesex County Commissioner and Chair of Economic Development Committee Chanelle Scott McCullum. “As a Board, we invest in culture to not only better the lives of our residents but also to bolster the local economy. People will travel miles to visit us for this event, and I have no doubt that this year’s stellar line-up will draw crowds from all over the Northeast. It’s going to be unforgettable!”

Year after year, this family-friendly Gospel Music Festival has featured legendary artists including Hezekiah Walker, Jekalyn Carr, Fred Hammond, Kierra Sheard-Kelly, and notable local talents such as The Jenkin Brothers, Lenore Davis, David Cross, Tawanda Muslim, and many others.

Middlesex County serves as a state-designated Regional Folklife Center, supporting the cultural and traditional expressions of the County and Central New Jersey. The FolkLIVE event series, including the Gospel Music Festival, not only underscores the County’s commitment to honoring its residents' diverse cultures but also fosters inclusivity and acceptance across communities. This is part of Middlesex County's broader investment and effort to ensure that arts, culture, and history are accessible to all residents. The Regional Folklife Center at the Arts Institute of Middlesex County is a project of the New Jersey State Council on the Arts, a partner agency of the National Endowment for the Arts.

For full details on the 2026 Gospel Music Festival and more cultural programming, please visit middlesexcountyculture.com.

posts.title: Pastor Turner Walk 40 Miles from Underground Railroad Site to Trenton, Spotlight Petition Demanding Passage of Two Reparations Bills
posts.author: Bridget Papino
posts.summary: LAWNSIDE, NJ / TRENTON, NJ — Rev. Dr. Robert Turner, pastor of Empowerment Temple AME Church and a Commissioner with the National African American Reparations C…
posts.content: LAWNSIDE, NJ / TRENTON, NJ — Rev. Dr. Robert Turner, pastor of Empowerment Temple AME Church and a Commissioner with the National African American Reparations Commission (NAARC), completed a 40-mile walk today from the Peter Mott House — a documented Underground Railroad site in Lawnside — to the New Jersey State Capitol in Trenton. The walk, the 46th in his ongoing "40 Miles for 40 Acres" campaign, drew attention to an active petition — citing New Jersey's status as the last northern state to abolish slavery — that calls for passage of two bills now before the Legislature. The walk was preceded by a community talk on the evening of Monday, July 13, at the historic Burlington Quaker Meeting House & Center for Conference in Burlington, NJ — a site where Friends have gathered for over 300 years. Rev. Turner discussed his book, Creating a Culture of Repair, and the history behind Walk #46; members of the press were invited to meet with him beforehand. The petition, which is still gathering signatures, points to New Jersey's standing as home to the largest documented Black-white wealth gap of any state — $662,500 in median household wealth for white families compared to under $20,000 for Black and Latino families — along with a homeownership gap (76.6% white versus 41.3% Black) that has barely moved in a decade, and the nation's worst Black-white incarceration disparity, with Black residents incarcerated at 12.5 times the rate of white residents despite comprising only 15% of the state's population. It calls on the Legislature to pass A1665, establishing a New Jersey Reparations Task Force, and A5253, the Truth, Reconciliation, and Repair Act of New Jersey, which moves beyond study to a framework of acknowledgment, accountability, and redress. The petition notes that reparations task force legislation has been introduced and failed in New Jersey five times — in 2005, 2019, 2022, 2024, and now again as A1665 — even as more than fifteen municipalities, including Newark, Orange, and Essex County, have already passed local resolutions in support. "We do not walk alone. We walk with a movement," the petition states, organized in solidarity with a coalition that includes the New Jersey Institute for Social Justice, Salvation and Social Justice, the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) of New Jersey, the New Jersey Reparations Council, NJ Faith Allies — Say The Word, Faith in New Jersey, the New Jersey Coalition of Religious Leaders, UU FaithAction NJ, and the African Methodist Episcopal Church — itself born in New Jersey as an act of resistance to racial injustice. "Acknowledgment without accountability is incomplete," said Rev. Turner. "The path to genuine repair runs through Trenton." The petition will continue collecting signatures in the weeks ahead before being formally delivered to legislators.

posts.title: Tampa's Creatology Residency Week Returns for 5th Year, Launching $4,000 Creative Roots Fund for Emerging Creatives
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: Founded by Tampa native and creative entrepreneur Janelle "J'Nelle" Richardson, Creatology was born from a simple but powerful belief: "Creatives don't let other creatives create alone."
posts.content:
TAMPA, FL — In a world where many creatives are expected to build their dreams in isolation, Creatology Residency Week continues to prove that community is one of the most powerful resources a creative can have.

Returning July 6–11, 2026, Creatology Residency Week celebrates its fifth year of creating intentional spaces for artists, entrepreneurs, musicians, designers, writers, content creators, and visionaries to connect, collaborate, heal, learn, and grow together.

Founded by Tampa native and creative entrepreneur Janelle "J'Nelle" Richardson, Creatology was born from a simple but powerful belief: "Creatives don't let other creatives create alone."

What began as a small gathering has evolved into a six-day residency experience featuring networking opportunities, wellness programming, creative workshops, live performances, industry conversations, resource connections, and community-building experiences designed specifically for the creative community.

One of the most impactful initiatives this year is the Creative Roots Fund, an effort dedicated to investing directly into creatives through financial assistance and creative development opportunities.

The organization is currently seeking support and funding to award a total of $4,000 in scholarships to two to three deserving creatives during the Celebrate Creatives Day Awards Ceremony on July 11, 2026.

The week will conclude with Celebrate Creatives Day, a special recognition honoring creatives who continue to shape the cultural fabric of the Tampa Bay and surrounding regions. Last year, July 11 received an official proclamation recognizing Celebrate Creatives Day in the Tampa Bay and surrounding areas.

Residency Week programming includes:
- Virtual Kickoff Tap-In
- Mind Over Medium
- The Plug Room
- Creative Circle
- Culture Jam Sesh
- HITLab
- Celebrate Creatives Day Awards Ceremony
- Creative Roots Fund Scholarship Presentations

As Creatology enters its fifth year, its mission remains unchanged: to build spaces where creatives can find connection, opportunity, encouragement, and the resources needed to thrive.

For media inquiries, interviews, sponsorship opportunities, scholarship support, or event registration, please contact:

Kylie Humphrey
Outreach Liaison, Creatology Residency Week
Website: https://loveyourvoice101.com/creatology/       Email: itscreatology101@gmail.com

posts.title: WAJ Magazine Has a Brand New Home
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: After 10+ years and 42 issues, WAJ Magazine is now fully independent with its own home at wajmagazine.com — built for the creatives, entrepreneurs, and community voices we've always existed to amplify.
posts.content:
For over a decade, WAJ Magazine has told the stories of the people shaping culture in New Jersey and beyond — the artists, the entrepreneurs, the athletes, and the community leaders who don't always get the spotlight they deserve.

Today, we're proud to launch our own independent home at wajmagazine.com. Every issue we've ever published, all 42 of them, is now available right here — both as digital downloads and physical print copies you can hold in your hands.

This is more than a new website. It's a new chapter. WAJ Magazine is growing into a full media brand with its own blog, its own features program, and its own voice — while staying true to where we started: two friends from Bergen County who believed the people doing the real work in our community deserved a real platform.

Want to be featured? Have a story to tell? We're opening submissions to our community — whether you're an artist, a business owner, an athlete, or someone doing meaningful work where you live. Submit your story and our editorial team will take it from there.

Thank you for a decade of support. Here's to the next one.

posts.title: Honey Bxby Covers Issue 042 — New Jersey's Own

posts.content:

Issue 042 is available now in both digital and print. Grab your copy and see why New Jersey keeps producing some of the most compelling voices in culture today.

posts.title: We're Opening Submissions — Get Featured in WAJ Magazine
posts.author: WAJ Editorial
posts.summary: WAJ Magazine has officially opened community submissions for our Features program. Merit-based selection, no payment required — just real stories from real people.
posts.content:
Since 2014, WAJ Magazine has been built on one core belief: every community has voices worth amplifying, and most of them never get asked to share their story. We're changing that in a bigger way.

We've officially opened our Features submission program to the public. Whether you're a musician, an entrepreneur, an athlete, a community organizer, or someone doing something meaningful that the world should know about — we want to hear from you.

Our selection process is entirely merit-based. There is no payment required to submit, and no payment required to be featured. Our editorial team reads every single submission and selects features based on your story, your impact, and your connection to the culture and community we cover.

Head to our Features page to submit your story. If selected, our team will reach out within 30 days to take things further.

This is your platform. Use it.
